items.title: Boosting Wnt Signaling Reverses APOE4 Alzheimer’s Damage
items.snippet: APOE4 suppresses Wnt signaling in oligodendrocytes, trapping fats in lipid droplets and breaking down brain insulation in Alzheimer's.

items.title: How Stress Reactivates Arthritis
items.snippet: Scientists discover how psychological stress reactivates arthritis flares via a sympathetic nerve-brown fat axis that sends IL-6 to dormant joints.

items.snippet: A psychedelic compound found in magic mushrooms appears to have an unexpected effect: calming highly aggressive fish. Researchers discovered that low doses of psilocybin significantly reduced aggressive attacks in mangrove rivulus fish without disrupting their normal social interactions. items.title: Eating blueberries every day may have a surprising effect on your mood
items.snippet: Eating blueberries every day could have surprising effects on mood, according to a small study that found greater reductions in depressive symptoms among older adults who consumed the fruit for three months. Researchers also detected changes in gut microbial enzymes, suggesting a possible gut-brain connection, although the mood benefits were not statistically significant compared with a placebo.

items.snippet: Researchers have uncovered three brain pathways linked to lasting improvements in people receiving deep brain stimulation for severe, treatment-resistant depression. They also discovered that patients who failed to improve after two years shared a striking pattern: insufficient stimulation of a crucial brain connection. items.title: Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
items.snippet: Scientists have discovered a surprising two-way relationship between sleep and growth hormone, revealing how the brain carefully balances physical recovery with wakefulness. The findings could help explain why poor sleep harms metabolism and brain health, potentially opening the door to new treatments for sleep and neurological disorders.

Should We Look to Hunter-Gatherer Societies as Models of Equality?
items.snippet: On the shores of Lake Eyasi in Northern Tanzania, a small number of people still hunt and gather their food. Today a Hadza hunter has taken down an animal—a kudu. He can’t carry it by himself, so he cuts his poisoned arrow from its flank, covers the carcass in dry grass to hide it from hyenas, and heads home to enlist help. News spreads like wildfire across the camp. Everybody rushes to the kill.

items.title: Scientists link a strange sugar in red meat to a 63% higher diabetes risk
items.snippet: A study of nearly 90,000 adults found that people consuming the most of a little-known sugar found in red meat had a 63% higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Scientists suspect the sugar may trigger chronic inflammation, potentially revealing a hidden connection between red meat and diabetes that goes beyond weight gain.

items.title: New drug reverses severe fatty liver disease by repairing the gut
items.snippet: Scientists have discovered that a potential new drug can reverse severe fatty liver disease in animal models by restoring gut health and blocking harmful substances from reaching the liver. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments for liver disease and potentially other serious conditions, including cardiovascular disease.

items.title: USC scientists discover how to create a never-ending supply of cancer-fighting cells
items.snippet: USC scientists have discovered a way to create a potentially renewable supply of genetically engineered immune cells that can attack cancer and strengthen the body's natural defenses. By growing and modifying immature immune cells rather than mature ones, researchers developed a system that can continuously produce tumor-fighting cells inside the body.

items.title: Scientists discover how exercise reverses muscle aging
items.snippet: Scientists have uncovered a hidden biological mechanism that helps explain how exercise can reverse some of the damage caused by muscle aging. The key is a gene called DEAF1, which becomes overactive with age and interferes with the muscles’ ability to clear damaged proteins and repair themselves. items.title: Eating late at night linked to up to 30% higher risk of liver disease
items.snippet: Eating late at night could be putting your liver at risk, according to a large study led by Oregon Health & Science University. Researchers analyzed data from nearly 200,000 people and found that those who regularly ate after dinner or around bedtime had a 20% to 30% higher risk of liver disease, including fatty liver disease and cirrhosis.
